title: Water in winter
summary: Melt snow and ice before you drink them and treat them, keep water and pipes from freezing, and drink before you feel thirsty.
doFirst: No heat and below freezing? Shut the main valve, catch the water as you drain the pipes, then leave the faucets open.
Don’t eat snow or ice: melt it first, then treat it.
Never use a camp stove indoors, or inside a tent or snow shelter.
Drink often, before you feel thirsty.

list: Don’t eat snow or ice to quench thirst. It lowers your body temperature (National Weather Service), and your body has to use energy to melt it, which can lead to more dehydration (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Ice gives more water than the same amount of snow and needs less heat to melt (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Use fresh, clean snow (Army ATP 3-50.21). Skip yellow snow (urine, pollen or sand), pink or red snow (algae) and snow with dirt in it (Scout Life, Boy Scouts of America).
Snow and ice are no purer than the water they came from (Army ATP 3-50.21). Treat melted snow and ice like any other wild water.

steps: Put a little water in the pot first, then add the snow. It melts faster and the pot won’t scorch (Scout Life; Army ATP 3-50.21: adding water to snow helps it melt faster).
Plan fuel for it: in winter you may need a stove to melt drinking water, because streams may be frozen over or buried (Yosemite National Park, National Park Service: streams may not be accessible).
On a sunny day, snow or ice spread on a dark cloth or sheet in the sun melts with no fuel (Army ATP 3-50.21). Catch the water in a container.

blocks.warn: Melt snow on a camp stove, grill or charcoal only outdoors. Never use a charcoal grill, hibachi, lantern or portable camping stove inside a home, tent or camper (CDC), or inside a snow shelter. Never burn charcoal indoors (CDC). Carbon monoxide can kill.

list: Keep stored water in the warmest part of the house you can, above freezing: CDC says to store it at 50°F to 70°F (10°C to 21°C).

Water expands when it freezes and can break its container. Leave 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) of air space at the top of anything that may freeze, and use plastic: some glass breaks even with the space (Ohio State University Extension).
Outdoors in the cold, store water containers upside down so you can still use them when the water freezes (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Keep your water filter from freezing: freezing can damage it (Colorado State University Extension).
Very cold water needs double the bleach (CDC, EPA). With iodine in icy water, wait at least 1 hour (Yosemite National Park).

blocks.p: In an unheated house, pipes can freeze and burst, and a frozen pipe may already be broken and leak when it thaws (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, adapted from the American Red Cross).
First save the water that is in the pipes, the water heater, the toilet tanks and a well’s pressure tank.
When the heat fails in freezing weather, Purdue Extension says to protect the plumbing like this:

steps: Shut off the water at the main valve, or turn off the well pump if it is in the house.
Drain the pressure tank, if you have a well.
Open all the faucets until they drain completely.
Drain the toilet flush tanks and spray hoses.

Empty the drain traps of sinks, tubs, showers, toilets, washtubs and floor drains, or pour in propylene-glycol antifreeze, as much as the water in the trap: 1 pint to 1 quart (0.47 to 0.95 L), depending on the size of the trap.

Turn off the power or fuel to the water heater and other appliances that use water, and drain them, including the pumps of the washing machine and dishwasher. Don’t put antifreeze in appliances or in the water supply pipes, only in drain traps.

blocks.warn: Never put car antifreeze (ethylene glycol) in any part of a home water system (Purdue Extension).

blocks.p: Before you thaw a pipe, know where the main water valve is: the pipe may already be broken and leak as it thaws. If it does, shut the main valve until the leak is repaired. Keep electric cords away from water (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, adapted from the Red Cross).

Then keep its faucet open and warm the frozen part with a heating pad, a hair dryer, an electric portable space heater or towels soaked in hot water, until full water pressure is back (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, adapted from the Red Cross).

blocks.warn: Never thaw pipes with a blowtorch, a kerosene or propane heater, a charcoal stove or any other open flame. They are a serious fire hazard and give off deadly carbon monoxide (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, adapted from the Red Cross).

blocks.label: Toilets when the water is off

list: Cold weather dulls your thirst and makes you pass more urine, so you can become dehydrated without noticing (Human Performance Resources by CHAMP; Army ATP 3-50.21).
Staying hydrated is one of the best things you can do to prevent cold injury (Human Performance Resources by CHAMP).
Don’t wait to feel thirsty: drink often (Human Performance Resources by CHAMP). Dry winter air means you need more water; don’t forget to drink because it’s cold out (Yosemite National Park).

On long days out, take in salt and other minerals as well as water, from food or an electrolyte drink, not salt tablets (Dehydration protocol): too much plain water can cause dangerously low blood sodium (Human Performance Resources by CHAMP).
